source.title: Self-awareness of impairment and the decision to drive after an extended period of wakefulness

confidence_rationale: The only paper in this pull that documents a genuine overconfidence effect emerging under extended wakefulness, with a rough timescale anchor (self-rated impairment onset ~19h into continuous wakefulness, tracking a PVT-measured decrement equivalent to 0.05% BAC). Confidence held at only 0.55 because the effect is COMPARATIVE (self vs. a hypothetical other), not calibration-based (confidence vs. own accuracy) -- a materially different construct from SD-076's running self-accuracy estimate, and from the null findings in the two Baranski entries above.
failure_signatures: Participants consistently rated a hypothetical OTHER person's driving ability as worse than their own under the same conditions of extended wakefulness -- the overconfidence here is a self-other comparative bias, not a drift in the accuracy of self-assessment per se; self-ratings of one's OWN driving ability DID decline roughly in step with objective PVT performance, which is the opposite of what a pure calibration-drift account would predict.

The authors' own concluding concern is about the GAP between self-rating and other-rating, not a demonstrated failure of self-calibration -- so this paper should not be read as establishing that waking self-accuracy confidence becomes miscalibrated; it establishes something narrower and different, a social-comparison optimism bias that happens to co-occur with fatigue.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Over 40 hours of continuous wakefulness, participants' self-rated driving ability declined significantly in step with objective psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) performance, with the first significant decline appearing around 19 hours of wakefulness; participants nonetheless consistently rated a hypothetical other person's driving ability as worse than their own under identical conditions.
mapping.ree_translation: REE reads this cautiously as the one piece of evidence in this pull for a genuine overconfidence-type phenomenon under extended wakefulness, and as a rough timescale anchor (order ~19h into a wake episode) that could bound the exposure-budget question in GOV-FANOUT-1's H2. But the specific overconfidence documented here is a self-vs-other comparative bias that coexists with reasonably accurate self-calibration (self-ratings tracked PVT decline), not a runaway inflation of the self-accuracy estimate SD-076 encodes -- so it should not be over-read as direct magnitude evidence for SD-076's construct.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a comparative-optimism paradigm (self vs. hypothetical other), which is a structurally different construct from SD-076's asymmetric running-variance EMA over one's OWN accuracy history. The paper's own data show self-ratings tracking objective decline reasonably well, which if anything argues against a large self-calibration drift and for the Baranski findings above -- the 'overconfidence' language in the abstract refers to the self-other gap, not a self-calibration failure. Treating this as support for SD-076's magnitude should be done with real caution.
mapping.source_context: 32 healthy adult humans, 40 hours of continuous wakefulness, self- and hypothetical-other driving-ability ratings every 2 hours alongside the Psychomotor Vigilance Task, laboratory setting.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality moderate: reasonable N and design, mid-tier chronobiology venue. Mapping fidelity is the binding constraint and is low: the documented effect is a self-other comparative bias co-occurring with accurate self-calibration, not the self-calibration drift SD-076 posits, so this paper's 'supports' rating is for the general phenomenon of wakefulness-linked overconfidence rather than for SD-076's specific mechanism.
